hook.line: Nobody likes saying no or giving bad news, and in Bogotá a blunt "no" can land hard. A short opener softens it before the bad part arrives.
hook.es: Me temo que no va a poder ser este mes.
hook.en: I'm afraid it won't be possible this month.

examples.es: Me temo que no va a poder ser este mes.
examples.en: I'm afraid it won't be possible this month.

examples.es: Me temo que va a ser difícil.
examples.en: I'm afraid it's going to be difficult.

examples.es: Me temo que la abogada ya salió.
examples.en: I'm afraid the lawyer has already left.

examples.es: Me temo que no tenemos mesa.
examples.en: I'm afraid we don't have a table.

examples.es: Me temo que va a ser imposible.
examples.en: I'm afraid it's going to be impossible.

examples.es: Me temo que Vale no va a poder venir.
examples.en: I'm afraid Vale won't be able to come.

rule:
*Me temo que* means "I'm afraid that..." in the polite sense of "sorry to say". It is not about being scared.

After *que*, say the bad news with an ordinary verb: *no tenemos mesa*, *ya salió*. No special ending is needed here.

Spanish also likes to soften with *va a ser* ("it's going to be"): *va a ser difícil* sounds kinder than *es imposible*. And *no va a poder ser* is a gentle, standard way of saying no.
smallPrint: Teachers call this a mitigating phrase: it lowers the force of what comes next. *Temerse* here is about regret, not fear.

readAndPick.es: Me temo que va a ser difícil.
options: I'm afraid it's going to be difficult.
I'm scared of the difficult one.
It was difficult.

readAndPick.es: Me temo que no va a poder ser este mes.
options: I'm afraid it won't be possible this month.
I'm afraid it wasn't possible last month.
I hope it will be possible this month.

readAndPick.es: Me temo que la abogada ya salió.
options: I'm afraid the lawyer is about to leave.
I'm afraid the lawyer has already left.
I hope the lawyer has left.

readAndPick.es: Me temo que no tenemos mesa.
options: I'm afraid we have a table.
I'm afraid we don't have a table.
We are afraid of the table.

readAndPick.es: Me temo que va a ser imposible.
options: I'm afraid it's going to be impossible.
I'm afraid it was impossible.
I think it's possible.

readAndPick.es: Me temo que Vale no va a poder venir.
options: I'm afraid Vale will come.
I'm afraid Vale won't be able to come.
Vale is afraid I can't come.

readAndPick.es: Me temo que Hernando no está.
options: I'm afraid Hernando isn't here.
Hernando is afraid I'm not here.
I'm afraid Hernando is here.
I'm afraid we will close soon.
I'm afraid we're already closed.
I hope we closed.

readAndPick.es: Me temo que no tengo tiempo hoy.
options: I'm afraid I don't have time today.
I'm afraid you don't have time today.
I'm afraid I had time today.

yourTurn.prompt: Pick *es* or *va a ser* and type the softer sentence: *Me temo que ___ difícil.*
yourTurn.answer: Me temo que va a ser difícil.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: I'm afraid it won't be possible this month.
yourTurn.answer: Me temo que no va a poder ser este mes.
accept: Me temo que este mes no va a poder ser.
yourTurn.why: *No va a poder ser* is the gentle way to say no.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: I'm afraid we don't have a table.
yourTurn.answer: Me temo que no tenemos mesa.
yourTurn.why: After *me temo que*, the bad news uses an ordinary verb: *tenemos*.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: I'm afraid the lawyer has already left.
yourTurn.answer: Me temo que la abogada ya salió.
yourTurn.why: *Salió* is the ordinary past, with no special ending.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: I'm afraid Vale won't be able to come.
yourTurn.answer: Me temo que Vale no va a poder venir.
yourTurn.why: *No va a poder* plus the infinitive *venir*.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: I'm afraid it's going to be impossible.
yourTurn.answer: Me temo que va a ser imposible.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: I'm afraid I don't have time today.
yourTurn.answer: Me temo que no tengo tiempo hoy.
accept: Me temo que hoy no tengo tiempo.
yourTurn.why: Same frame, new news: *no tengo tiempo hoy*.

pitfalls.wrong: Tengo miedo que no va a poder ser.
pitfalls.right: Me temo que no va a poder ser este mes.
pitfalls.why: Almost. For "I'm afraid" in the polite sense, Spanish uses *me temo que*.

pitfalls.wrong: Me temo que no tengamos mesa.
pitfalls.right: Me temo que no tenemos mesa.
pitfalls.why: Almost. Here *temerse* reports bad news as a fact, so the verb stays ordinary.

pitfalls.wrong: Me temo no va a poder ser.
pitfalls.right: Me temo que no va a poder ser este mes.
pitfalls.why: Almost. The bad news after "I'm afraid" always needs *que*.

personal: Give a friend some mild bad news about your schedule, starting with *Me temo que*.
